what_it_does: When you run a neural network on a chip, each layer's numbers are rounded down to fewer decimal places (a process called quantization) to save memory and speed things up. The question is: how many decimal places should each layer keep? Using the same level for every layer wastes precision where it is cheap and loses accuracy where it matters. This paper proposes CLADO, a method that first learns — on a small sample of data — how rounding errors in one layer ripple into other layers downstream (something prior methods ignored). It then solves a math optimization problem, specifically an Integer Quadratic Program (a standard solver that finds the best combination of whole-number choices), to assign each layer its own ideal precision level. The result is a better accuracy-versus-chip-cost trade-off than methods that assume each layer is independent.
